To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) phonology has an effect on lexical categorization; (ii) the effect is stronger on the verb class than the noun class; (iii) the effect is not due to phonological similarity to other words of the same lexical category, but is due to phonological markedness.

(1) phonological information plays an important role in determining the category of a word, (2) this role can be accommodated within Cognitive Grammar by means of phonological sub schemas, (3) the phonological sub schemas proposed by Cognitive Grammar do not yield clear predictions vis à vis empirical data.
the semantic and phonological properties of a word are the most reliable predictors of its lexical category, and that phonological properties can be used to distinguish nouns from verbs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the human brain processes language, and how this knowledge can be used to improve the Cognitive Grammar model of language.

the following issues: (i) the role of semantics, distribution and phonology in lexical categorisation; (ii) how the model of Cognitive Grammar can accommodate the available data; (iii) whether the model can predict new data; (iv) whether the model is empirically adequate; (v) whether the model should be modified to account for the available data.
the question of how to integrate the phonological, distributional, semantic, and conceptual dimensions of word classes in the Cognitive Grammar framework.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is not yet in, and the issue is still open.
the semantic basis is more important than the formal one, but the formal one is also important and should be taken seriously.
nouns and verbs are defined in semantic terms, but with the proviso that the semantics is not the only relevant factor, and that phonology is also a significant contributor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
phonology, semantics, syntax, and pragmatics all contribute to the lexical category of a word.
the cognitive linguistic model of word classes is more robust than the formalist model, but that the former needs to incorporate the phonological data that the latter already takes into account.
nouns and verbs have different phonological properties, and these properties are important in lexical categorisation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
phonology is a necessary component in the model of lexical semantics.
Cognitive Grammar should not only be based on semantics but also phonology.
the cognitive linguists' emphasis on semantics is not in conflict with the traditional distributional approach to word classes; rather, it complements and extends it.
